As sunlight enters the atmosphere, it collides with tiny gas molecules such as nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules are much smaller than the wavelength of visible light, so they scatter the light in a process called Rayleigh scattering. The Moon shows phases because it does not shine on its own; it reflects sunlight. At any moment, the Sun lights up one half of the Moon, while the other half is dark. As the Moon orbits Earth, the angle between the Sun, Moon, and Earth changes, so the amount of the illuminated half that we can see from Earth changes too.

When the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, the lit side faces away from us, so we see little or none of it. That is the new moon. As the Moon moves along its orbit, a thin crescent of the lit side becomes visible, then more of it appears during the first quarter and waxing gibbous phases. When Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, the entire near side facing us is illuminated, producing a full moon. After that, the visible lit portion gradually decreases through the waning gibbous, third quarter, and waning crescent phases until the next new moon.

This full cycle takes about 29.5 days. Importantly, ordinary lunar phases are not caused by Earth’s shadow falling on the Moon; they are simply a result of our changing viewing angle of the sunlit portion. Earth’s shadow is involved only during a lunar eclipse, which is a separate event.

Salt melts ice on roads by lowering the freezing point of water, a phenomenon known as freezing-point depression. Road salt, usually sodium chloride, does not warm the ice directly. Instead, when it contacts ice, it dissolves in the thin film of liquid water that is often present on the surface. That creates a salty solution, or brine, whose freezing point is lower than that of pure water.

In pure water, molecules arrange themselves into an orderly crystalline structure as they freeze at 32°F (0°C). Dissolved salt releases sodium and chloride ions that interfere with this orderly arrangement, making it harder for water molecules to lock into solid ice. As a result, the water can remain liquid at temperatures below the normal freezing point. If the ice and the brine are in contact, ice continues to melt until the system reaches a new balance consistent with the lower freezing point.

This is why salt is effective for deicing roads: it helps convert existing ice into liquid and can prevent new ice from forming onto the pavement. Its usefulness depends on temperature, because very cold conditions can make even salted brine freeze. Different salts, such as calcium chloride or magnesium chloride, can work at lower temperatures because they depress the freezing point even more strongly. Salt is effective, but it is only useful within certain limits and can also have environmental and corrosion effects.

Onions make people cry because, when they’re cut or crushed, they release sulfur-containing compounds that irritate the eyes.

In an intact onion, those compounds are stored inside cells separately from the enzymes that can turn them into irritants. Once the cells are damaged, the enzyme alliinase breaks down the sulfur compounds and helps produce a volatile gas called syn-propanethial-S-oxide. A few things can reduce the effect, like cutting onions under running water, using a very sharp knife, chilling the onion first, or working in a well-ventilated area. Cooked onions usually don’t cause the same reaction because the enzymes and irritant are largely broken down by heat.

Onions make people cry because of a chemical defense mechanism that is triggered when the vegetable is damaged. An intact onion stores sulfur-based compounds inside its cells, along with enzymes that are kept separate from those compounds. When you cut, chop, crush, or bite an onion, the cell walls break and the enzymes come into contact with the sulfur compounds. This starts a chain reaction that produces a volatile irritant known as syn-propanethial-S-oxide.

This irritant evaporates easily and travels through the air to your eyes. When it reaches the moist surface of the eye, it stimulates sensory nerve endings in the cornea. The nerves send a signal to the brain, which interprets the sensation as irritation or burning. In response, the lacrimal glands produce tears to flush the irritant away and protect the eye.

In other words, the tears are not an emotional reaction; they are a protective reflex. The amount of irritation can vary depending on the onion variety, how finely it is cut, and how fresh it is. Some onions release more of the lachrymatory compound than others, while milder varieties produce less. Chilling an onion before cutting can also reduce vapor release, and using a sharp knife helps minimize cell damage, which may lessen the irritation. Wearing goggles, cutting near running water, or using a food processor with a sealed lid can further reduce the amount of irritant that reaches your eyes.

Cats purr for several reasons, and the behavior is more complex than simply signaling happiness. A purr is produced when a cat rapidly contracts and relaxes the muscles in its larynx, or voice box, causing the vocal folds to vibrate as air moves in and out during breathing. This creates the low, steady rumbling sound people associate with a contented cat.

One major reason cats purr is communication. Kittens often purr while nursing, which may help reassure the mother, and mother cats may purr to soothe their young. Adult cats frequently purr when they are relaxed, being petted, or curled up near a trusted person, so purring can certainly indicate comfort and affection.

However, cats also purr in less obviously “happy” situations. They may purr when they are sick, injured, stressed, or even near death. In those cases, the vibration may serve as a self-soothing behavior or as a attempt to communicate distress. Some researchers also suggest that the low-frequency vibrations of purring may have physical benefits, such as promoting healing in bones and tissues, though this idea is still studied rather than fully settled.

In short, cats purr for a mix of emotional and physiological reasons. It can express contentment, strengthen social bonds, calm a kitten, or help a cat cope with pain or stress. The same sound can therefore mean very different things depending on the context.

Airplanes fly because their wings generate **lift**, an upward force that counteracts gravity.

A wing is shaped and angled so that, as the plane moves forward, air flows faster over the top of the wing than under the bottom. This creates a difference in air pressure: lower pressure above the wing and higher pressure below it. The result is an upward push on the wing.

Another way to think about it is that the wing **deflects air downward**. By Newton’s third law, the air pushes back up on the wing. Both effects—pressure differences and downward deflection of air—help produce lift.

For an airplane to stay airborne, lift must at least balance the plane’s **weight**. The engines provide **thrust**, which moves the plane forward and helps it maintain the speed needed for lift. As the plane travels, it also experiences **drag**, the resistance of the air, which the engines must overcome.

Pilots control flight by adjusting the wings and tail surfaces, changing the amount of lift and the direction of travel. In steady cruising flight, the forces are balanced: lift equals weight, and thrust equals drag. That balance is what allows an airplane to fly smoothly through the sky.

A spoon looks bent in water because of refraction: light changes direction as it passes from one medium to another. The short version is that the light coming from the submerged part of the spoon is bent at the water’s surface, so your eye receives it along a path that does not match the spoon’s actual position.

More specifically, light travels slower in water than in air. When a ray of light leaves the water and enters the air, it bends at the boundary. If you are looking at a spoon partly submerged in a glass, the underwater section sends light to your eye along rays that have been refracted. Your brain tends to interpret light as if it traveled in a straight line, so it projects the apparent source in the wrong place. That makes the submerged part of the spoon look higher or shifted compared with the part above the water, creating the illusion of a bend at the waterline.

The effect is not because the spoon is actually deformed. It is simply a visual artifact caused by the way light behaves across the air-water boundary. The exact amount of apparent bending depends on the viewing angle, the depth of the spoon, and the liquid’s refractive index, but the basic principle is the same in everyday situations.

def solve(record):
    edges, source, target = record['record_1']

    def normalize(name):
        return name.strip().casefold() if isinstance(name, str) else name

    queue = deque([start])
    distances = {start: 0}
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        for neighbor in graph.get(node, ()):
            if neighbor in distances:
                continue
            distances[neighbor] = distances[node] + 1
            if neighbor == goal:

            queue.append(neighbor)

    return None
